subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS-COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, July 2, consideration in committee of bill No. 193, to amend the Combines Investigation Act-Mr. St. Laurent-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 4-Transfer from D.T. & I.C. Act of provisions re certain complaints.

subtopic: MONOPOLISTIC TRADE RESTRICTIONS-COMBINATIONS IN RESTRAINT OF TRADE
speechtext:
In reference to section 4, this matter of combines and restraints of trade came up a few years ago in connection with 63260-195
sections 498 and 498 (a) of the criminal code. There had been an indictment and some appeals before the authorities in Ontario in connection, I believe, with milk, electrical, contractors, agreements of manufacturers to sell exclusively, and also as to heat, light and power corporations, and a bill of indictment was laid before one of the assizes. Meetings had been held of various companies fixing prices and agreeing as to who should tender on certain contracts in connection with municipal work, and the question was raised as to the applicability of sections 498 and 498(a) of the code, which are referred to on page 233 of Snow's Criminal Code and the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act, 1935, to these particular combines. One of the cases went to the privy council, and it was held that these combines could not be regulated in this manner.
Combines in restraint of trade have been flourishing like a green bay tree under all governments since confederation. The sections of the code were found to be of doubtful effect. Why were they invalid and unworkable? Because they were made a football between the attorney general of Canada and the attorneys general of the provinces. I remember that in the 1926-27 session, on the Ottawa-Georgian Bay bill, on March 14, 1927, these particular matters were brought into issue regarding navigable streams, as to which rights were international and which interprovincial, and the jurisdiction of the dominion over boundary waterways schemes and interprovincial schemes. Unfortunately the bill was talked out at that particular session. These proceedings will be nothing but a farce, because you cannot by the widest stretch of imagination exercise any control over these international cartels. Security and social councils, so far as international regulation of combines goes, are a myth. I know, because I had some experience with the super-power trust for a good many years. It was contended by a former member for South York, Mr. Maclean, who was a very valuable member of this house and also a powerful newspaper man in Toronto, and I agreed with his contention, and submit it now to the right hon. gentleman who is leading the house, that it is the duty of the federal government to enforce its own law in relation to these combines that operate in restraint of trade. The reason for that is obvious; such combines come almost exclusively under the control of this parliament, since by section 91 trade and commerce are within its jurisdiction.
As regards the principle of referring these questions to the attorneys general of the provinces, I do not know how it got into the

Combines Investigation

act, but I contend that it has been fatal to the whole procedure. I have nothing but the greatest respectfor Mr. McGregor, having had a good deal to do with him in the days when he was an officer of the Department of Labour. He is all right, but the whole of this law is all wrong. We do not exercise over combines the same effective control that the Sherman Act exercised years ago in the United States, because under that act the president and others who have to do with its enforcement can take real action; and they have not our complicated division of powers under the British North America Act.
I suggest that the greatest step forward in the regulation of trusts and combines in this country was taken by the government of Mr. Bennett when he appointed the price spreads committee in 1933-34, on the membership of which sat my hon. friend representing the constituency of Haldimand (Mr. Senn). That committee accomplished something that had never been done in the history of this parliament. It made a real investigation into the operation of combines in restraint of trade. It summoned all interested parties; all sides of the question were debated; witnesses were heard representing trade and commerce and restraint of trade, and the committee submitted a very valuable report. It astonished the working classes of Canada to learn what was going on in the country in this respect. The report of that committee was the key to the whole situation.
We know very well how divided the attorneys general of the provinces are in matters of this kind. This was fully recognized by the former member for South York, Mr. Maclean, back in 1924, 1925 and 1926, and I have always agreed with the view he expressed that the federal law in regard to trade and commerce, and jurisdiction over combines in restraint of trade, should all be under the control of the attorney general of Canada, who should initiate proceedings, instead of leaving it to the provinces themselves, who have no jurisdiction.
Sections 498 and 498A were in the code before we had a commission and before the department was given the power it now has under the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act of 1935, and these particular sections have been before the law courts of the country for consideration. The cases are set out at page 233 of Snow's Criminal Code. One of the cases even went to the privy council. If this parliament really wishes to do something about combines it should put the power to enforce the law where it belongs. These combines and restraints of trade are flourishing like a green bay tree. We all know

what the American super-power trust has meant in connection with waterways in the United States. Private ownership had control of the whole thing and Ontario was finally redeemed from slavery by the government that came into office in the province in 1905. It gave the joy and boon of cheap light and power to people in the cities and in the suburban and rural parts, and domestic and commercial lighting in consequence costs nearly three times less than it did before. In my opinion, the government is not going about this problem in the right way. This is not the way to attack combines. These combines will go on as long as there is such a thing as trade and commerce, because you cannot stop restraints of trade by legislation in which clever lawyers can find loopholes whenever the need arises. I was president of the union of Canadian municipalities for some time and this whole question came up in the municipal association in Toronto. We had a full discussion of it then and I do not believe that under this bill we are going to make any progress at all in controlling combines because, as I say, lawyers can find a loophole in any act. A lawyer can go to the attorney general of the dominion and say: This is a purely provincial matter which should be referred to the attorney general of the province; and the result will be that the whole thing will become a political football. As I have already pointed out, the Sherman law in the United States has enabled those in authority to take effective action. The ratepayers of that country have been given the real picture.
See what has happened to the bank act. You can drive a coach and four through this act just as you can through the bank act. There is a section of the bank act that declares that banks shall not deal in real estate. Why then should it be necessary for a bank to have a thirty-five storey building to do work that could be done on four floors? Where have the attorneys general been so far as that is concerned? I suggest that the same thing is going to happen here under the Combines Investigation Act. I fail to see how combines are going to be regulated by this legislation unless the enforcement is by the attorney general of Canada.
But not being able to regulate combines in restraint of trade in our own country, they want to branch out now and regulate and control cartels in international affairs. They want to take in the seven seas. But the people are waking up and are finding that little or nothing can be done about it. I appreciate the fact that in Mr. McGregor we have a valuable officer, but Mr. McGregor cannot

Combines Investigation
do anything unless he is given proper enforcement machinery. Section 4, the bill states in the explanatory page, is substantially similar in form to section 20, chapter 59, of the statutes of 1935, the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act. Provisions of that act, which make its section 20 applicable to the combines investigation act and to sections 498 and 49SA of the criminal code, are proposed to be repealed by subsection 1 of section 14 of this bill. In my opinion this will mean nothing so far as regulating combines is concerned. If- we want to regulate combines effectively we must bring them within the jurisdiction of the criminal code, and to do that we must make the sections really effective. Before a bill can be laid before the assizes, section 4 must be invoked, and sections 498 and 498A of the code, and if you take the case to the law courts, after investigation by the Minister of Labour, you will find that you are wasting your time, because I doubt whether a bill of indictment would be laid before the grand jury. And if it were, it would no doubt be quashed later in the courts.

speechtext:
Last evening the
minister made reference to certain changes which I suggested, and he indicated that if certain restrictive provisions "which the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen put in there in 1935-" and I add "were removed"-"I will agree to take out the provision restricting the laying of information to the attorneys general". I have quoted from the minister's statement at page 3073 of Hansard. I do not know of any record in support of the minister's statement. I hold in my hand the senate report of July 3, 1935, in which any recommendations for changes which were made in the bill as submitted to the senate committee were introduced, and concurrence was moved not by the Hon. Mr. Meighen but by the Right Hon. Mr. Graham, who presided over the committee. I mention that by way of clarification. Nowhere have I been able to find any suggestion, either in the banking or commerce committee to which the matter was submitted, or in the debates in the senate, which would bear out the statement that in fact it was Mr. Meighen who introduced the proviso that prosecution should not take place under section 498 of the criminal code and at the same time under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act.
With regal'd to section 10A, when the commissioner is led to believe that there is a combine or a merger which contravenes the provisions of the act, does he proceed with the taking of evidence, either under oath or 63260-195i
not under oath, or how does he determine the question upon which a prima facie conclusion is arrived at that a combine does in fact exist? I took the trouble to read over the evidence of the banking and commerce committee of 1937, and it was interesting to note that one of the recommendations made was that as soon as any information came to the chairman of the tariff board which indicated that there was a combine in any particular commodity, that information should be communicated to the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. Last evening I was surprised to learn that as to radio tubes and sets, although the tariff board found in 1939 and 1940 that Canadian consumers were being unduly exploited through the arrangements then in effect, no information of that kind was brought to the attention of the commissioner. This is a serious matter. The supply of small radios has been clearly restricted by the actions of a combine operating not only internationally but in Canada.
Last evening I asked the minister what he was going to do about it. What is he going to do about the findings of the commissioner on the electric lamp combine? What is he going to do about the findings of the commission as to radio tubes and sets? There fes no doubt the findings are clear and definite-that there is a combine and that the Canadian, consumer is being exploited. What does he? intend to do about matches and the othe;r matters referred to in the report?
Under section 10A-and this is supposed to consolidate the section in the dominion trade and industry commission act and also in the criminal code-the commissioner may receive and investigate complaints and communicate them to the attorney general of the province or to the attorney general of Canada. Does that mean that^ he shall investigate them and communicate his findings, or is it merely permissive? So far as the crown is concerned I realize that "may" is mandatory. But is it not a fact that under these circumstances the word "may" makes no action mandatory on the part of the commissioner? I should appreciate it if the minister would explain general^'- the procedure. In the banking and commerce committee of 1937 one of the chief complaints was that, while there were preliminary investigations, little serious action was taken on the basis of the information secured by the commissioner. The time has come for a declaration by the minister as to the extent to which wrongdoing revealed in this report is to be proceeded against. I realize the difficulty with international cartels, hut what about the cartels operating in

subtopic: CLARIFICATION AND EXTENSION OF PROVISIONS AND BENEFITS
speechtext:
I thought that this afternoon, as the hour is getting late, I might make a statement which I have before me, and perhaps hon. members would like to discuss the principle of the bill after they have heard the statement. I have drafted it in a manner which I hope will make it easier for hon. members to understand the rearrangement of the act and also certain sections of the act, and certain fundamental changes which are being made in it.
Five years ago, on July 1, 1941, contributions under the Unemployment Insurance Act first became payable. Now that we are considering a number of changes in the act to make it work more smoothly and to close some of the gaps which have appeared, it is perhaps well to take stock of what has been accomplished in order to place this important piece of social legislation in its true perspective. Many hon. members doubtless have read statements made in another place or on May 23 on the second reading of the bill. At that time some interesting statistics were placed on the record, and I will not repeat them at this time. However, I am sure you will be interested to know why it has been considered desirable to introduce the bill in this house, and the reasons why it was withdrawn from the other chamber.
Subsequent to the decision of the government to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, it was decided to add sections to the bill which would involve expenditures of money.
These amendments relate principally to veterans and certain merchant seamen.
It may be well to recall that the Canadian unemployment insurance scheme is based on sound insurance principles, many of which are common to both commercial and social insurance.
The first of these is that there must be a reasonable interest in a contingency.
In the case of an employee, this contingency is his contract of service which may fail in its completion bjr a lay-off, by termination in accordance with its own terms, or by mutual agreement.
The second of these principles is that the indemnity or benefit arising out of the contingency must be related to, but must not exceed, the loss or value of the insurable interest.

Unemployment Insurance
The benefit may be related to part of the loss, as in some forms of automobile insurance, or a cash benefit related to, but less than earnings, as in unemployment insurance.
The third principle is that due weight must be given to what might be called the moral hazard. In commercial insurance this would result in a selection of risks, but in the wider scope of unemployment insurance results in the erection of proper safeguards in the public interest.
These past few years have proven an extremely difficult time. in which to recruit and train a staff to man the local and other offices of the commission. I think it can fairly be said that a good job has been done, although we are continually endeavouring to improve our standards. The continual training of staff on the job is expected to result in a still higher degree of efficiency.
We are operating a public service of the greatest importance by seeking to match jobs with those seeking jobs, while at the same time ensuring that claims against benefit rights accumulated in the war years are handled promptly and equitably.
The act became effective at a good time in so far as the building up of the fund was concerned. Employment climbed steadily, resulting in almost one-fifth of the papulation of Canada having a direct stake in the fund. With their dependents, this means more than 50 per cent of the population of Canada. This has helped to cushion these months of changeover and adjustment.
The effect of any social legislation is dependent on the extent of the classes of persons covered. In July, 1941, there was insured under the Unemployment Insurance Act almost all employment in industry, apart from the basic industries of agriculture, fishing, lumbering and logging, transportation by water and air, which presented special problems, as well as those excluded by reason of the wage ceiling of two thousand dollars.
It has been and still is the policy of the government to widen the scope of the act as rapidly as possible, and the changes effected, together with those projected, indicate the progress being made.
In January, 1942, action was taken by order in council to retain within the insured classes persons whose earnings exceeded two thousand dollars a year because of war conditions, such as increased hours and other factors.
In that same year action was taken to place veterans in as nearly as possible the same position as they would have had under the act had they not served in the armed forces.
This step was made effective by the postdischarge reestablishment order, is now in the present bill and will become part of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
It provides that employer and employee contributions, for the period of service in the forces subsequent to June 30, 1941, will be paid into the unemployment insurance fund by the government when the veteran completes fifteen weeks in insured employment in any period of twelve months following his discharge. This is proving a most satisfactory and realistic way for veterans to build up a share in the fund.
The only previous bill amending the Unemployment Insurance Act was passed in July, 1943, and effective from September 1 of that year the ceiling for salaried employees was raised from $2,000 to $2,400, to take care of the general rise in earnings.
In place of the order in council insuring those whose earnings were higher because of the war, the earnings ceiling was removed entirely for persons paid by the hour, day, week or on a piece rate.
The other change in coverage made at that time was the inclusion of all employees of public utilities who were within the insurable earnings limit, so as to remove discrimination between municipally-owned utilities and those owned by private companies. Previously, municipalities had been allowed exception for certain of their permanent employees.
Here let me say a word on this question of permanency of employment and coverage under the act. There are those who feel that where there is little risk of unemployment, the employment should not be insured.
On reflection, it will be quite clear that if those who were fortunate enough to have stable employment were excluded, it would be virtually impossible to build up a fund adequate to provide benefit for those with less stable employment without making the amount of the contributions prohibitive. It is only by spreading the risk that a sound scheme is possible. The man who pays his fire insurance premium and does not have a fire is fortunate.
Then even in employments regarded as most stable, unemployment is not unknown. In Britain, in the nineteen-twenties, when their unemployment insurance act permitted the withdrawal from the general scheme of industries which were thought to be particularly stable, the coal mining industry considered setting up a special scheme. The heavy unemployment suffered in that industry in the years that followed is only too well known.
Unemployment Insurance

Included in the 1943 amendments was one giving the governor in council authority to extend coverage to excepted employments on joint recommendation of the commission and the unemployment insurance advisory committee. This has made it possible to extend the scope of the act without waiting for an opportunity to introduce a bill into parliament.
Thus, in August of last year, employment in transportation by air and as a professional nurse (other than employment as a private duty nurse or as a probationer) became insurable.
Following a series of investigations into the peculiar problems, both seasonal and administrative, of lumbering and logging in different parts of the country, action was taken to make employment in this industry insurable.
Contributions are to commence in British Columbia on August 1 of this year. It is expected that in a comparatively short time the industry will be insured' across the country.
Discussions are now under way for further extensions in coverage by joint recommendation of the unemployment insurance commission and the advisory committee. However, there is now included in the bill an amendment which will make insurable employment in transportation by water-both inland and deep sea.
Until reciprocal arrangements have been completed with the United States and Great Britain, our coverage of deep sea vessels will be somewhat limited, but a start is being made and it is fully anticipated that proper arrangements can be made with these other countries as to the jurisdiction over vessels of different registry.
Many persons insured under the act are now faced for the first time with the need to take advantage of the benefit rights which they have been accumulating, and I think it may be of general interest to outline the handling of claims.
At the outset let me emphasize that the first action taken when an unemployed person enters the local office is to register him for employment and inform him of the employment opportunities which are available.
Only after this has been done are the necessary forms completed for the filing of a claim, if the insured person so desires.
A claimant must deposit his unemployment insurance book, or arrange to deposit it when he files a claim; he is required to give particulars of his employment during the previous six weeks, in order that the reasons for separation from employment may be verified. There is a disqualification imposed, for

example, if a claimant has left his employment voluntarily without just cause, or he has been discharged because of misconduct.
If the claimant wishes to receive benefit at the higher rate because he maintains a dependent within the meaning of the act, further particulars must be provided. He must give details of any spare-time occupation which he follows, because there are restrictions in the act governing the receipt of benefit by persons with spare-time jobs.
A claimant is ordinarily required to report once a week in order, to prove unemployment, capability of work and availability for work. He may be called in during the week because of an employment opportunity which has arisen. On his weekly reporting day, the placement officer must certify that there is no suitable employment available for him, before action is taken to record his unemployment.
There are a considerable number of claimants who live at too great distances from any local office to file claims in person. The practice is to permit such persons to file their claims by mail if the cost of return transportation from their home to the nearest local office exceeds thirty cents; they are then called "postal claimants." They not only file their first claim by mail, but they continue to report weekly by mail. Their statements as to unemployment, et cetera, must be certified by two responsible individuals. The payment of benefit is made by cash in the larger local offices and in the remainder, by warrant. Postal claimants are paid by warrant.
The contribution records of insured persons are maintained at eight points across the country. The contributions in the current insurance book, together with those in the records for a period of two years preceding the claims, determine the rate of benefit. Similarly contributions recorded for the five years previous to the claim, and benefit paid in the preceding three years, determine the duration of benefit.
The adjudication of claims is the responsibility of insurance officers appointed under authority of the act. These officers are located at numerous points across the country.
The main questions which an insurance officer must decide in adjudicating claims for benefit are whether the required contribution conditions have been fulfilled; if the claimant left his employment voluntarily, did he have just cause for so doing? Was he discharged for misconduct within the meaning of the act? Or does his unemployment result from a stoppage of work due to a labour dispute? Also, a claimant must be sixteen years of age and a resident in Canada before he is entitled to benefit.

Unemployment Insurance
Let us look at the important and controversial subject of suitable employment. The act specifies certain types of employment which are not to be considered suitable, for example, employment which arises out of a stoppage of work due to a labour dispute, employment which would require a claimant to become a member of, or to refrain from becoming a member of a union.
The act also states clearly that employment is not to be regarded as suitable if it is employment in the claimant's usual occupation where the wages are lower or the conditions less favourable than those observed by agreement between employer and employee. Neither is employment suitable in another occupation where the wages are lower or the conditions less favourable than those he obtained in his usual occupation.
On the other hand, it is likewise specifically provided that after a lapse of a reasonable interval from the commencement of unemployment, employment in another occupation is not to be considered unsuitable (in other words it is suitable) if the wages offered are not lower and the conditions not less favourable than those obtaining in that occupation.
It is only possible to consider whether a particular offer of employment is suitable in relation to an individual claimant at that time; what is not suitable to-day may well be suitable a month from to-day. The most careful consideration has been given to the guidance afforded insurance officers in adjudicating cases of refusal of employment which is apparently suitable, and reference has been made to both British and American experience in handling this problem.
Some of the factors considered by insurance officers are the difference in the rate of wages between the usual occupation and the work offered; whether there would be any sacrifice of skills in accepting the job offered; the length of unemployment; whether there is any prospect of the claimant finding work with his former employer within a reasonable time, or whether there is any possibility of his finding work in what is his usual occupation.
After an accident, for instance, a man may not be able to return to his former work, and he must consider a change in occupation immediately. Or a man who has reached retirement age for a given occupation cannot hold out for employment of that kind. Similarly, there are certain skills which were required during the war which have little or no place in a peacetime economy. Then there are always circumstances peculiar to an individual	claimant-his family responsibilities. adaptability, age and so on, which affect his suitablity for a job.
Let me emphasize that in no country has it been found practicable to legislate on what is suitable employment, because it is one thing one day for one claimant, and something else a month or two hence. It should always be remembered that if a claimant is not satisfied with an insurance officer's decision, he has a right of appeal to a court of referees, composed of representatives of employers and employees, and an independent chairman. In certain circumstances there is a right of appeal to the umpire. Gradually there is being built up from decisions of the umpire a most important and helpful guide to the interpretation of various provisions of the act, which is of great assistance in striving for uniformity of action among those adjudicating claims.
Glancing over the amendments in this bill, hon. members will notice that nearly two-thirds relate to changes in references made necessary by a rearrangement of some of the sections and by minor clarifications of old .sections, which experience has shown as desirable.
Of the other changes, I wrould draw hon. members' attention particularly to the following:
Clause 3 of the bill permits coverage of persons whose status as employees has given rise to some argument; for example, men paid on a commission basis may be either employees or independent contractors. On the other hand, clause 36 excepts from coverage a person who is virtually an employer; for example, a man who owns more than half the registered stock of a corporation.
Clause 6 of the bill permits repeal of section 23(2) of the act if the present proposal in the bankruptcy bill on priority of claims is approved.
Clause 7 is a major rearrangement of the present section in order to set out in a more straightforward manner the conditions on which benefit will be paid. It also increases the earnings permitted from subsidiary employment from $1 to SI.50 a day; widens the group of dependents in respect of whom the increased benefit rate may be paid; authorizes benefits to 'be calculated to the nearest five cents, and also permits small errors to be cleared from the books of the fund. Clause 7 takes up about one-third of the bill.
Clauses 10 and 11, together with part of clause 7, clarify the question of appeals to the umpire.
Part of clause 14 assures that benefits obtained by false pretences will not be retained by the claimant.
Unemployment Insurance

Clause 16 extends the time in which proceedings for an offence may be commenced from three months to twelve months of evidence of .the offence coming to the knowledge of the commission.
Part of clause IS permits benefit to be paid where contributions were not paid due to an erroneous decision of an officer of the commission.
Clause 20 grants authority to pay expenses which may be incurred if it becomes necessary to pledge securities held in connection with the fund.
Clause 21 makes the date of the report of the advisory committee the same date as that of the commission.
Clause 22 permits gradual extension of coverage to lumbering and logging.
Clause 23 makes the national employment service responsible to the minister and permits it to carry out additional duties not within its formal functions.
Clause 24 transfers to the act sections of the Veterans Rehabilitation Act dealing with unemployment insurance, with some enlargement relating to veterans of allied nations and certain merchant seamen. In this connection clause 32 repeals the relative sections of the Veterans Rehabilitation Act.
Part of clause 25 continues the requirements that employers report engagement of employees and that persons seeking employment notify the employment service.
Clauses 33 and 34 extend coverage to merchant seamen.
I would like to deal in some more detail with the principle of ministerial responsibility suggested in respect of the employment service.
The efficient administration of' the Unemployment Insurance Act requires an effective employment service. The problems of war made it abundantly clear that a national employment service has other important functions to fulfil. The complexity of post-war conditions, the conviction that employment must be provided for all who want to work show that the employment service has still to play a much larger part in our national economic life than that connected with unemployment insurance.
The national employment service should and must become a keystone in the carrying out of plans of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Reconstruction, the Department of Transport, the Department of Agriculture and the Departments of National Defence in their various activities for reconversion and reestablishment.
There must be the closest possible working arrangement between departments at the ministerial level, and the Minister of Labour

must have detailed knowledge and control over the employment service so that he can give his colleagues the cooperation necessary to carry the reconversion plans to a successful conclusion.
Then there are cases where special financial or other curative measures are necessary. Such cases include employment problems of youth, of older persons who are not pensionable, of persons not covered by unemployment insurance, as well as problems associated with apprenticeship, and encouragement of movements of manpower to agriculture (one of the most important responsibilities we face at this time), basic industries or domestic service. More efficient dominion-provincial arrangements to deal with these matters would be possible where the minister could issue direct instructions to the employment service.
In the administration of the employment service and unemployment insurance, Great Britain has divided authority at the top level between a ministry of labour in charge of employment, and a ministry of national insurance in charge of unemployment insurance and other social security benefits. The long experience of Great Britain in matters of this kind makes worthy of note her action in determining this to be the most desirable line of action between parliament and the administrators concerned.
In the United States, the department of labour and the social security board have each had a hand in administration of the federal employment service, which in turn are separated from the state unemployment compensation authorities. At present, there is a move on foot to vest complete control of the employment service in the department of labour.
In New Zealand, the employment service will come under a newly created ministry of employment. Their social security department, which will be responsible for unemployment compensation policy at top levels, will have no authority over the employment service. Australia is to follow New Zealand's lead with a. commonwealth employment service directly responsible to the minister of labour and national services, and free to act independently of the department of social services.
Thus the plan proposed for Canada follows the trend that experience in other parts of the world has found desirable in that it seeks to make the employment service directly responsible to the Minister of Labour, rather than to have the chain of authority directed through the unemployment insurance commission.
It should be noted that sixty per cent of the money voted by parliament for the activities carried out by the staff of the commission is spent for work not covered by the act.

Questions
If this sixty per cent is a responsibility of the minister, it is submitted that it is the duty of the minister to exercise supervision of the employment service, because it is through that service and by its staff that money voted is spent.
Unemployment insurance and the employment offices are a part of the general social security programme. They are primarily concerned with one of the most important fields of national welfare, the provision of insurance payments during periods of unemployment and the movement through the employment offices of persons in search of gainful employment.
It has facilities to deal with veterans and to meet the problems of persons requiring vocational guidance, or special attention due to physical handicap. It is already taking its proper place in the minds of both workers and emploj'ers, a place which they see is necessary in any plan to maintain a high and stable level of employment.
I imagine that most people have had contact with the employment service during the war, particularly when national selective service was in full operation.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that you call it six o'clock.
